1228424537248817154 [2020-02-14] @m_ashcroft 💜 85 🔁 6
1/ Your sense of self and how you hold yourself physically are the same thing. They change with each other.

If you're like most people, you're holding in your belly right now. What happens if you let go? How are you different, now?

Let's play with this. (thread)
↓
1228424538603606018 [2020-02-14] @m_ashcroft 💜 19 🔁 1
2/ At some point in our childhoods, we formed a deep association between how we look and who we are.

We tried to look cool as we stood and walked. 
We sat up straight to look obedient and impress teachers.
We furrowed our brows to convey concentration.
↓
1228424540763627521 [2020-02-14] @m_ashcroft 💜 19 🔁 1
3/ As adults it's the same. 

We stand at the bar nonchalantly to look/feel relaxed. 
We puff out our chests to look/feel imposing and important. 
We hold in our bellies to look/feel slim and desirable. 

Those habits become who we are. But what if we stop?
↓
1228424542143623168 [2020-02-14] @m_ashcroft 💜 23 🔁 1
4/ Well, how's your belly? Holding it in again? Let go.

It's not easy. It can feel vulnerable, unsettling and unfamiliar. When you let go of the physical holding, you literally become someone different. You become someone who doesn't hold their belly in.

https://t.co/b3CIvJ8ZAR
  [Quoting Tweet 1227938022513086464 (missing)]
↓
1228424544773382144 [2020-02-14] @m_ashcroft 💜 33
5/ The mind and body are the same system. It's all one psychophysical thing - there's no such thing as a purely mental action and there's no such thing as a purely physical action.

When I teach Alexander Technique, I don't just reorganise bodies, I invite deep identity change.
↓
1228424547315130368 [2020-02-14] @m_ashcroft 💜 40 🔁 2
6/ Alan Watts identified this phenomenon. He said that the ego, the self, the sense of 'I' is a distinct pattern of muscular tension. 

When you allow the muscular tension, the holding, to stop, you also let go of your sense of I. It's the same process. 

https://t.co/cya1nAXvVd
  [Quoting @m_ashcroft: 18/ I have a theory here inspired by Alan Watts.   "It's a chronic habitual sense of muscular strain which we were taught in the whole process of doing spontaneous things to order." [6:30]   The video is worth listening to in full. Alan gets it.  https://t.co/7FrKx3a6g3]
↓
1228424549932421120 [2020-02-14] @m_ashcroft 💜 24 🔁 1
7/ I've seen people burst into tears, laugh deeply, and suddenly see solutions to major life problems. 

All I did was help them stop doing all the habits, all the effort, all the holding, all the trying to be someone that defined who they thought they were all their lives.
↓
1228424552474124288 [2020-02-14] @m_ashcroft 💜 20 🔁 2
8/ Who is the man who always puffs out his chest if he stops doing it?

Who is the woman who holds in her belly to look slim if she stops doing it?

That's moment of "uh oh, this is new and scary" is the point at which real change can happen.
↓
1228424553774436352 [2020-02-14] @m_ashcroft 💜 27 🔁 1
9/ This is why Alexander Technique is so powerful. It's not about posture. 

It's a mechanism for deep personal transformation by releasing a lifetime of held structures. 

It allows the natural and authentic expression of who you are when you aren't trying.

How's your belly?

Utility is high for practitioners but requires experiential understanding—outsiders may find it mystical without embodied practice.

title: The Superman clip that became a posture religion
summary:
Michael Ashcroft (@m_ashcroft) accidentally found the most viral way to explain Alexander Technique: a 30‑second Christopher Reeve moment where Clark Kent “does” smallness and Superman “non-does” into full height. The core claim that hooked people is dead simple and kind of spooky: Reeve doesn’t “straighten up” — he stops performing Clark, and the confident posture just *happens* when awareness expands.

Arc is basically: **[trigger]** Ashcroft posts the Reeve clip (Feb 2020) as “non-doing” → **[peak]** everyone starts laundering their own self-help frameworks through “Clark vs Superman mode.” @visakanv turns it into a vulnerability/bravery thing (“to stand at your full power is to reveal yourself as Superman… relax your shoulders and guts… contracted to protect you from the world”). @nosilverv riffs with “Drop Doings,” pushes it toward ego/enlightenment talk, and Ashcroft leans in hard: “Doing = ego… I’ve experienced kensho through AT,” plus the wild flex that the ‘enlightenment’ thing is “conveyed through touch.” Then Ashcroft deepens it with the identity claim: “your sense of self and how you hold yourself physically are the same thing,” with the belly-holding-in example as the tangible demo.

**[outcome/current state]** It doesn’t turn into a big fight; it turns into infrastructure. Ashcroft writes an article because the clip “was so resonant,” keeps re-bumping the thread for new followers, and it gets ported off-Twitter via @eigenrobot’s podcast episode (“awareness… game theory… and Superman”). Years later it’s still living as shared shorthand: @Malcolm_Ocean jokes his height changes depending on “clark kent mode or superman mode,” and @nosilverv repackages it as a general rule (“standing tall… automatically happens when you open your awareness”), with Ashcroft replying “yes” + linking the clip again. The residue is basically a meme-able diagnostic tool: stop trying to “fix posture” and instead notice what persona you’re tensing into — and whether you can drop the doings long enough to float back to full height.
